newsitem.title: GERMANY: Metro applauded for results, strategy.
newsitem.headline: Metro applauded for results, strategy.

text.p: German retail giant Metro AG, born out of a merger with three store chains last year, impressed investors on Tuesday by hitting 1996 profit targets and said it would seek to grow its business internationally.
Metro said its group income on ordinary activities was 1.062 billion marks ($627.1 million), while debut net profits came in at 717 million marks.
Profits calculated on the DVFA accounting standard were a touch lower at 712 million marks, putting DVFA earnings per share at 7.10 marks. The company gave no comparative figures.
"I must say that the results surprised me and are very positive," Vereinsbank's Max Resch said after retail analysts were briefed by Metro management.

Metro stock climbed sharply on the results and held onto most gains to end floor trading on the Frankfurt stock exchange up six marks at 184 marks -- the highest close since the merged group's first listing last August.
Resch raised his profit forecasts by 50 pfennigs a share to 11.50 marks for 1997 and to 12.80 marks for 1998. He expected Metro to outperform the broader stock market.
He added Metro looked cheap in relation to other German retail stocks, with a 1998 prospective price/earnings ratio of 14.4, compared to an average sector rating of 17.
Swiss-controlled Metro, Europe's largest diversified retail group, said it was satisfied with the results after sales came in unchanged at 62 billion marks.

The company, which owns the Kaufhof department store chain and MediaMarkt electronics business, said it expected sales to increase by three billion marks this year. Income on ordinary activities should also rise in 1997, CEO Michael Wiegandt said.

"This result expectation is based on our conviction that we will improve results in our business areas, lossmakers will no longer be part of the group and that we still can realise further merger synergies," Wiegandt said.

Metro announced it would propose to the annual general meeting a dividend on ordinary shares of two marks with a two mark bonus, while preferred shares would get a payout of 2.25 marks plus a two mark bonus.

Metro also said it planned to raise its equity capital via a seven-for-five share issue backed by drawing on capital reserves. Through the capital increase, the company's equity would rise from 501 million marks to 1.203 billion marks.

Vereinsbank's Resch said the issue would amount to "quasi-free shares", lowering the price of shares and making them more attractive to investors. Wiegandt said Metro would seek to maintain effective dividend continuity.

Looking ahead, Wiegandt said economic transition in western Europe would cause consumer demand to stagnate or even fall in the next 10 to 15 years. Meanwhile, Metro wanted to cater to eastern Europe, where purchasing power is rising and consumers are "discovering new shopping forms overnight".

Wiegandt said Metro would be interested in taking over AVA Allgemeine Handelsgesellschaft der Verbraucher if it became available. Investments this year will total 1.9 billion marks, of which 670 million marks are earmarked for abroad -- going to Poland, Turkey and China.

Commenting on the performance of individual units, Metro said its electronics shops, department stores and boutiques had all done very well last year. Metro's cash and carry business also reinforced its dominant position.
Metro wholesale pulled in 420 million marks, Kaufhof earned 203 million marks and MediaMarkt shops 240 million marks.

Furniture, however, lost 125 million marks after efforts to cut losses failed to meet objectives. Metro said it had sold its Moebel Unger unit effective July 1 to a group of investors and will take a 190 million mark charge on the sale this year.
Profits also fell short of expectations at Metro's building stores (187 million marks), shoe shops (25 million) and its Vobis computer stores (46 million), the company said.
